abstract: |
  The lack of standards for the equitable distribution of accessibility complicates efforts to address transport poverty. This study presents a model-based approach for selecting equity standards. This is done by exploring the relationship between objective accessibility and two employment-related variables for a sample of residents in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, Canada. We use objective accessibility calculated for three modes of travel (active transportation, public transit, and private vehicles) and other individual-level variables to estimate ordinal models. Further, we use spatial filters as instrumental variables to account for potential endogeneity. We examine the association between objective accessibility and the perception of having too few jobs available within an ideal commuting time (a perceived accessibility indicator) and the reports of having declined jobs because of transportation constraints (an employment outcome indicator). The results indicate that higher transit accessibility is associated with more positive perceived accessibility, whereas associations with active accessibility depend on whether respondents travel actively. Based on the results of these models, we identify accessibility thresholds that reduce the likelihood of negative perceptions and outcomes for transport-disadvantaged groups. We propose three thresholds that we classify as conservative, intermediate, and progressive. These thresholds are an example of a model-driven approach to support transportation planning in achieving more equitable outcomes, as well as for participatory processes to collectively define minimum or sufficient accessibility levels.

# Introduction

Transportation equity refers to the distribution of the burdens and
benefits of transportation systems among a population [@karner2020;
@pereira2017]. Burdens include health-related concerns arising from
exposure to air pollution, noise, and traffic; sedentary lifestyles; and
the risk of injury or death from collisions. In contrast, the primary
benefit is the provision of accessibility [@pereira2021], understood as
the ease of reaching (spatially distributed) opportunities and
destinations [@páez2012; @hansen1959; @soukhov2025], including
employment, healthcare, educational services, and venues for social
interaction.

Accessibility is one of the primary outcomes of spatial development
[@páez2012]. It is influenced by the spatial distribution of the
population and opportunities and depends on the characteristics and
performance of the transportation network. In other words, it is a
product of both transportation systems and land use patterns [@wee2011].
There is a growing consensus among researchers and transportation
planners that the goal of transport policy should be to improve
accessibility [@el-geneidy2022; @boisjoly2017], since activity
participation is one of the main ways in which transportation can help
to promote a dignified life [@karner2020; @dossantos]. In contrast,
insufficient or inadequate accessibility can prevent individuals from
engaging in activities that are meaningful to them, for reasons that are
beyond their control. This process is described in the literature as
Transport-Related Social Exclusion (TRSE) [@litman2024; @lucas2012;
@preston2007; @luz2022; @paez2009mobility]. Insufficient accessibility,
when combined with other forms of social and economic disadvantage, can
result in transportation poverty [@lucas2019; @luz2022]: the failure of
transportation and land use systems to provide access to essential
services, employment, and other activities. Transportation poverty
increases vulnerability among individuals who already face challenges
associated with age [@vandülmen2022], income [@allen2019], race
[@awaworyichurchill2020], gender [@murphy2023], disability [@upham2022],
among other factors [@kim2024]. With the suburbanization of low-income
populations, it is estimated that over one million Canadians live in
transport poverty [@allen2019].

```{=html}

proved problematic as movement becomes the measure of success, while

any initial increases in accessibility [@farber2011running]. In reality people travel to

and so accessibility is seen as a superior indicator of performance
[@pereira2023]. It is worth noting, however, that congestion is part of the everyday routine of many people and one

[@handy2020], which may help to explain why mobility-centered approaches

```

A challenge with the use of accessibility as a measure of transportation
poverty is the lack of standards for the equitable distribution of
accessibility [@soukhov2025a]. Additionally, there is an absence of
transportation data in the form of open data products to support urban
planners [@arribas-bel2021; @behrendt_mobility_2024; @páez2021], and
transportation planners receive limited formal guidance in assessing the
equity implications of their projects [@miller2018; @palm2023;
@tebrömmelstroet2016]. Furthermore, relatively few studies explicitly
link accessibility levels with the experience of accessibility, such as
employment opportunities declined or accepted due to transport
conditions, or the ease to reach employment opportunities within ideal
commuting times. Combined, this results in a gap in the development and
implementation of accessibility standards to ensure equity in
transportation planning and policy.

This study is guided by the following research questions: How do
objective job accessibility indicators, i.e., calculated based on
spatial and transport data, relate to perceived accessibility and to
self-reported employment outcomes? And could a given level of
accessibility serve as a standard or goal for equitable transport
planning? This study proposes a model-based methodology for defining
equity standards in transportation planning. We obtain these standards
from the estimated relationships between objective job accessibility,
people's perceived accessibility, and a self-reported employment
outcome.

While prior studies have examined the association between objective and
perceived accessibility [@pot2021; @lättman2016; @zhu2025], and between
objective accessibility and employment outcomes [@bastiaanssen2021;
@duarte2023; @jin2018; @johnson2017; @matas2010; @kain1968; @bania2008;
@delmelle2021; @merlin2017; @bastiaanssen2025], few have used these
relationships to derive accessibility thresholds (e.g., @negm2026).
Grounded in a transport equity perspective, the novelty of our work is
the use of a model-based approach to define accessibility thresholds
conditioned on individual characteristics, allowing standards to be
defined from the standpoint of a chosen reference profile. Specifically,
we define accessibility thresholds as the minimum levels at which the
reference profile becomes more likely to give a non-negative response
than a negative one, or, under a more demanding definition, a positive
response than a negative one. Although these thresholds are obtained at
the neighbourhood level, they indirectly incorporate individual-level
characteristics, since they are derived from individuals' self-reported
perceptions and outcomes.

This study is guided by an understanding of accessibility as a means
through which transportation can foster human dignity [@pereira2021;
@dossantos], combined with an egalitarian and sufficientarian view of
transportation equity. From this perspective, a fair transportation
system should guarantee a minimum, sufficient level of accessibility to
all members of society, with this sufficient level defined from the
standpoint of those historically and currently facing the greatest
transportation disadvantage [@martens2021].

After this introduction, we structured this article as follows: Section
2 provides a brief theoretical background on objective and perceived
accessibility, on the identified connections between objective job
accessibility and employment outcomes, and on the identification of
equity standards based on accessibility. Section 3 presents the
materials and methods, covering the study area and data sources, the
method used to calculate accessibility, how we modelled the relationship
between objective accessibility and the dependent variables, the process
used to identify equity standards, and how we measured transportation
equity based on these standards. Section 4 presents the results. Section
5 critically analyzes the paper and presents its limitations. Finally,
Section 6 concludes with final considerations.

# Theoretical background

## Objective and perceived accessibility

The most commonly used accessibility measures are based on the gravity
model of Hansen [-@hansen1959]. This model considers the number of
opportunities that a person can reach to be proportional to the sum of
opportunities in each destination, discounted by the travel cost to
reach that destination. This type of metric is classified as a
place-based measure [@pereira2023], representing a characteristic of a
given location that assumes that all people in this location have equal
access to the spatially distributed opportunities. For relying on the
use of spatial and transport data to create indicators, these measures
are referred to as calculated, spatial, location-based, or objective
accessibility; hereafter, we use the term *objective accessibility*.

However, objective accessibility does not take into account the
individual characteristics of people. The perceived accessibility, on
the other hand, refers to the perception of people of how easily they
can reach opportunities [@lättman2016; @pot2025; @mehdizadeh2025],
resulting from not only the interaction of land-use and transport
infrastructure [@geurs2004], but also from travel options (e.g., having
a car or a transit pass), travel experiences, and individual
characteristics and preferences. Often, perceived accessibility deviates
from objective accessibility, with some research indicating that
objective accessibility might not be able to capture the multiple ways
in which people experience a lack of access to opportunities [@zhu2025].
Explanations for these differences are partially attributed to
differences in individuals' travel attitudes, capabilities, and
preferences [@devos2025; @vandervlugt2022]. In addition, objective
measures often rely on travel time as the only impedance factor, while
other factors that might also shape individuals' perceptions of the ease
or difficulty of reaching destinations are not considered, such as
safety, comfort, and even enjoyment of the trip [@handy2001evaluating;
@handy2020].

Another factor that might impact the relationship between objective and
perceived accessibility is adaptive preference, in which political
oppression, poverty, and adverse social conditions distort the
preferences of individuals living in deprived circumstances
[@baber2007]. In this situation, someone with restricted financial
resources living in an area with low (objective) accessibility might
adapt their expectations and preferences to align with their
circumstances, and might therefore not consider their accessibility
levels to be insufficient [@negm2025].

Residential self-selection can also impact the relationship between
perceived and objective accessibility, in which people may choose their
residential locations based on travel needs, abilities, and
travel-related attitudes [@cao2009]. In fact, residential location
decisions differ across income groups, impacting the relationship
between objective job accessibility and employment status [@Hu2017].
For instance, high-income individuals often prioritize living in places
with low job accessibility because they prefer suburban housing
amenities, such as green spaces and larger homes, over proximity to
work, accepting longer commutes because they can afford - and might even
prefer to have - a car. As a consequence, their perceived ability to
reach employment opportunities may be defined less by their
neighbourhood's job accessibility and more by their resources and
preferences. On the other hand, low-income individuals might prefer to
live close to employment hubs to maximize their chances of having a job,
while reducing commuting and housing costs.

Objective accessibility is still commonly used to evaluate the effect
that the interaction between land-use characteristics and the
transportation system has on perceived job accessibility and on
employment outcomes. In addition, existing studies on perceived
accessibility seem to have difficulties in creating standardized
definitions and measurement tools, contributing to the somewhat limited
knowledge on the topic [@negm2025]. In this context, connecting
objective to perceived accessibility helps to capture non-spatial and
employment‑related barriers that are not visible in place‑based measures
alone, since the objective accessibility might be perceived differently
even between people living within that same neighbourhood. In this
paper, we define sufficient
levels of accessibility based on the relationship between objective
accessibility and people's perception of job accessibility and
employment outcomes, while also controlling for individual
characteristics.

## Job accessibility and employment outcomes

Studies connecting employment outcomes to job accessibility date back to
the 1960s, when John Kain [-@kain1968] proposed the spatial mismatch
hypothesis while analyzing Detroit and Chicago, USA. The author
hypothesized that the low employment rates among Black Americans in
inner cities resulted from employment decentralization and the
difficulty faced by the Black population in moving out of these areas,
primarily due to racial discrimination and segregation.

Since Kain [-@kain1968], studies linking objective job accessibility and
different employment outcomes have presented mixed results. Bania et al.
[-@bania2008] found no significant effect for job access when examining
its relationship with employment, earnings, hourly wage, and weekly
hours worked for women leaving welfare in Ohio, USA. Delmelle et al.
[-@delmelle2021] also found that changes in car accessibility had no
significant impact on employment rates for different population income
groups in the Metropolitan Area of Charlotte, North Carolina, USA,
arguing that the spatial separation between lower-wage workers and their
workplaces might already be relatively small. Studying Los Angeles, USA,
Merlin and Hu [-@merlin2017] found mixed-effects of job accessibility on
employment status, with a stronger association for more highly educated
groups. The authors argued that lower-educated groups may be more
limited by non-spatial factors that impede their employment
opportunities, such as qualifications, labour market readiness, and a
lack of social networks. On the other hand, for workers with a higher
level of education, the time and monetary costs of spatial separation
itself may play a relatively more important role, so accessibility
measures may have a greater impact on their decisions and ability to
enter the labour market.

In contrast, other studies found significant effects of job
accessibility on employment outcomes [@bastiaanssen2021; @duarte2023;
@jin2018; @johnson2017; @matas2010]. Jin and Paulsen [-@jin2018] used a
difference-in-differences model for the Chicago Metropolitan Area,
finding that increasing job accessibility between 2010 and 2017 was
associated with reduced unemployment rates. Duarte et al. [-@duarte2023]
found that job accessibility had a positive effect on participation in
the labour market for women, a negative effect on informal employment
for women, and a positive effect on the probability of being employed
for both women and men. More recently, Bastiaanssen et al.
[-@bastiaanssen2025] examined differential employment effects of job
accessibility by public transport in combination with the bicycle for
different educational groups at the national level in the Netherlands.
They found that jobs for lower-educated groups are often located outside
areas of high accessibility, thereby reducing job accessibility among
these groups, while jobs for higher-educated groups tend to be
concentrated in and around downtowns and are associated with greater
accessibility. In this study, the assumed connection between the spatial
dimension of accessibility and people's perceived accessibility and
employment outcomes is the basis for the identification of equity
standards.

## Equity standards

An equity standard, when operationalized, defines the level of fairness
to be adopted and the acceptable inequality [@soukhov2025a].
Accessibility standards typically combine a concept of fairness with
threshold criteria, reflecting both vertical and horizontal equity
approaches. Vertical equity is often operationalized through
opportunity‑based standards defined for specific population groups
(e.g., minimum access to opportunities within a 10‑minute walking trip
for older adults), whereas horizontal equity commonly appears in the use
of uniform travel impedance thresholds applied across all potential
users (e.g., a maximum acceptable distance to a transit stop).

@yenisetty2020 set an opportunity-based standard, considering a distance
of more than 1,200 meters between amenities, services, and facilities by
public transport to be unfair when analyzing cities in India.
@tiznado-aitken2018 defined unfair cases as those where bus stops and
metro stations are located more than 1 kilometer away. @sun2021 adopted
400 meters as the maximum acceptable walking distance to bus and tram
stops, and 800 meters to ferry stations in England. In another study,
@peungnumsai2020 identified opportunity standards through the ratio of
public transport supply to demand, considering conditions fair when
demand is greater than supply.

The use of different thresholds reflects the idiosyncratic manner in
which standards are developed, and the rationale for choosing a certain
distance to, for example, bus stops or train stations, is often unclear.
In addition, the use of distance-based thresholds may be problematic,
since the time required to cross a certain distance can vary
considerably within a city, even for the same mode of transportation. To
address this problem, we suggest standards based on key thresholds of
objective accessibility.

However, beyond making explicit how standards are defined, it is also
important to make transparent the moral principles that guide their
definition, because different theories of justice lead to different
perspectives on how policies should manage the distribution of
transport-related benefits. @pereira2021 argue that transportation
equity research benefits from linking two justice theories: Rawlsian
egalitarianism [@rawls1999] and the Capability Approach [@sen1979;
@sen1999; @sen2005; @sen2009]. Rawls' Difference Principle holds that
inequalities are only justifiable if they benefit the least advantaged
members of society, centred on the fair distribution of primary social
goods - resources and opportunities that every person needs to pursue
their life plans. Sen builds on this, arguing that the focus should
shift from primary goods to human capabilities: the opportunities
available to individuals and their freedom to choose and act,
recognizing that the same resource can translate into different real
opportunities depending on individual circumstances. Within
transportation research, accessibility to opportunities can therefore be
understood as a capability that enables participation in social,
economic, and community life [@pereira2017; @luz2022].

Both theories inform two moral perspectives commonly applied, though
rarely made explicit, in transportation equity research [@martens2016a;
@wee2011]. The sufficientarian perspective asks why some groups or areas
lack sufficient access, building on the idea of a minimum threshold of
accessibility required to meet basic needs, with priority given to those
falling below it. The egalitarian perspective instead focuses on
relative differences in accessibility between groups or areas, treating
unequal access as unfair regardless of whether a group's absolute access
level meets a minimum threshold [@pereira2021]. Applying either
perspective therefore requires identifying which groups are of concern:
the sufficientarian view asks who falls below the threshold, while the
egalitarian view asks between whom access differs.

In practice, this attention has centred on disadvantaged population
groups, including those affected by low income, limited ability, and
historical discrimination, which have become the focus of transportation
research [@lucas2019]. This is due to the potential of historical
discriminatory policies and other disadvantages to negatively impact
their transport experiences [@pereira2021]. Additionally, these groups
have often been excluded from the transportation planning process,
resulting in their needs frequently being not recognized. Within studies
that investigated associations between objective accessibility and
employment outcomes, relevant groups include youth, adults, women,
children, low-income individuals, zero-vehicle households, people with
disabilities, single-parent households, refugees, and racialized
populations [@bania2008; @Hu2017; @middleton2019; @tabascio2024].

In this study, we recognize accessibility as a human capability
[@sen2005; @sen1999; @pereira2017; @luz2022], something required for a
dignified life [@karner2020; @dossantos], and one of the main benefits
of transportation to be distributed across society in order to increase
people's freedom. Following the sufficientarian perspective, we define
equity standards as minimum accessibility thresholds required to reduce
the likelihood of negative perceptions and outcomes. Following an
egalitarian view, these thresholds are defined with particular attention
to transport-disadvantaged population groups. In doing so, the paper
presents an analysis that identifies minimum acceptable levels of
accessibility, discusses inequities in these values, and presents a
generalizable methodology for other geographical areas, populations and
opportunity types.

# Materials and methods

Our approach for obtaining equity standards of accessibility based on
the relationship between objective measures, people's perceptions, and
employment outcome can be synthesized in the following main steps:
modelling job accessibility, predicting individual perception and
outcome using objective accessibility, setting equity standards for
transportation, measuring transportation equity by using
Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) measures [@foster2010].

## Study area and data sources

The study area for this research is the metropolitan region of the
Greater Toronto Area and the Hamilton Area (GTHA), in Ontario, Canada.
More specifically, the study area refers to the Census Divisions of the
regional municipalities of Hamilton, Halton, Peel, Toronto, York, and
the Durham subdivisions within the Toronto Census Metropolitan Area
(Figure \ref{fig:study-area-map}). According to the latest census
[@statisticscanada2023], over 7.2 million residents live in this area,
which is spread across around 7,300 square kilometres.

```{r study-area-map, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=paste0("Map of the study area (population density is classified using quintile breaks).")}

knitr::include_graphics(paste0(figures_diretorio,"/location_map_v2.png"))
```

Regarding the primary data sources, this study uses data from two
different sources: the latest Canadian Census (2021) from Statistics
Canada to calculate objective accessibility; and the National Survey of
Transport Poverty (NSTP) from the Mobilizing Justice Partnership
[@tiznado-aitken] to obtain variables related to individuals' perceived
accessibility and employment outcomes. The Census was selected due to
its various socio-economic and demographic variables and due to the
"Commuting to Work" questionnaire, allowing the identification of
individuals in the labour force and including variables required to
calculate job accessibility, such as place of work, commuting modes, and
commuting duration. The Census also provides standardized spatial
datasets with statistical and administrative geographical boundaries,
including the Census Tract (CTs), which are used in this study as the
spatial units used for calculating accessibility measures (obtained
using the {cancensus} `R` package [@cancensus]). According to the Census
[@statisticscanada2023], 3,868,120 individuals in the labour force
reside in the study area, competing for a total of 3,043,730 job
opportunities.

The Census also provides the number of people in low income, which we
use to assess accessibility gaps among low-income residents. Low income
is defined using the Low-Income Measure, After-Tax (LIM-AT), a relative
threshold set at 50% of the median adjusted after-tax household income,
where each household's after-tax income is adjusted by dividing it by
the square root of household size. According to the 2021 Census, around
10% of the study area population lives in low income.

The second source of data, NSTP [@tiznado-aitken], is a large-scale
survey designed to understand TRSE and transport poverty in Canada. It
is a representative sample of more than 27,000 people aged 15 years and
older across the country, and it provides an unprecedented look at the
transportation challenges that Canadians face, especially among
transport-disadvantaged groups whose experiences are often overlooked.
The survey is openly available to researchers, decision-makers, and the
public, and offers information on household dynamics, respondents'
perceptions, and individual-level socioeconomic data. The NSTP provides
respondent weights to enable the creation of statistics that are
consistent and representative of the Canadian population. From this
survey we select variables corresponding to respondents' perceptions of
accessibility and employment outcomes, in addition to socioeconomic and
demographic variables at the individual level. The responses are
geocoded by place of residence and can be assigned to Census geographies
to link them to objective accessibility.

For this study, only a sample of the NSTP was used. This sample
corresponds to labour force respondents residing in the GTHA who
reported being able to work, whether they are employed or unemployed,
and who are not retired, sick, or on parental leave. Using a continuum
scale from 0 (completely disagree) to 100 (completely agree), the
respondents answered to what extent they agreed with the statements in
Table \ref{tab:out-description}, namely *"There are too few jobs
available for me in my ideal commuting time"* and *"I have had to
decline employment opportunities because of my transport situation"*. In
total, the NSTP sample refers to
`r length(respondents_design$variables$fexp_final)` respondents that
represent `r sum(respondents_design$variables$fexp_final)` individuals
in the labour force (weighted sample).

#outcome_descriptions_table

  kable_styling(font_size = 10)

```

### Objective accessibility inputs: labour force, job opportunities, and travel costs

Calculating objective accessibility, as operationalized in this paper
(see following section), requires three inputs: the number of
opportunities at each destination, the population competing for them at
each origin, and the cost of travelling between origins and
destinations, which is translated into travel impedance through a
mode-specific function.

Using microdata from the Census, we calculated for each CT the number of
people in the labour force that commute to work by walking, cycling,
private vehicles (those who commute by car, truck, or van as a driver or
passenger, and motorcycles or scooters), and public transit (those who
commute by bus, subway, light rail, streetcar, commuter train, and
passenger ferry). The labour force is defined as in the Canadian Census:
civilians aged 15 and older who are employed or unemployed. We
distributed remote workers according to the share of each transportation
mode in each CT. Then, we summed the number of jobs in each CT
considering the place of work mentioned by each worker.

We calculated the travel times between origins and destinations for each
travel mode using the {r5r} `R` package [@pereira2021a] with a street
network obtained from OpenStreetMap. We used the General Transit Feed
Specification (GTFS) obtained from the Canadian Public Transit Network
Database [@statisticscanada] to retrieve the public transit schedule and
coverage. Considering that our study area contains different transit
agencies, we evaluated the GTFS files to identify a common date/week
with public transit service. After this analysis, we set 8 a.m. (morning
peak time) of December 22, 2025, as the trip departure time. Although
this date falls during Christmas week, there were no differences in the
public transit service schedules of the transit agencies due to the
holiday, which makes this date representative of a regular weekday in
terms of public transit travel time estimation. We also used Digital
Elevation Models (DEM) from the Canadian Digital Surface Model (CDSM),
with a spatial resolution of about 20 meters, to estimate the effect of
declivity on walking and cycling times. For cycling trips, we defined a
standard level of traffic stress (LTS) as tolerable for most mainstream
adults. LTS defines the level of comfort or danger that a street
presents for cyclists based on speed limits, lane counts, and
infrastructure. The standard LTS defined in {r5r} [@pereira2021a]
includes bike lanes with physical separation from multi-lane or
higher-speed traffic. We set a maximum duration of 180 minutes (3 hours)
for private vehicles and public transit trips, with a maximum walking
time of 5 minutes to reach the vehicle and 15 minutes to reach the
public transit stop/station; for walking and cycling trips, we set a
maximum duration of 90 minutes (one and a half hours). After estimating
the travel times between CTs, we assumed that all intra-CT trip
durations are equal to 0.1 minute.

Commute duration was used to calibrate Probability Density Functions
(PDFs) to represent travel impedance, following the approach of Soukhov
and Páez [-@soukhov2024a], Verma and Ukkusuri [-@verma2025], and Dos
Santos et al. [-@dossantos2026], where the impedance value represents
the probability that the trip will occur given a specific travel time.
We used the {fitdistrplus} `R` package [@delignette2015fitdistrplus] and
tested different functional forms (uniform, negative exponential, gamma,
normal, and lognormal distributions) to select the best PDF for each
mode of transportation and municipality, using as the selection criteria
the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) value [@akaike1974]. The
estimated impedance functions appear in Appendix
\ref{tab:impedance_functions}.

## Calculating objective accessibility

In this study, we implement the multimodal spatial availability measure
of @soukhov2024. This measure is a constrained indicator of
accessibility that can account for multiple modes [see @soukhov2023;
@soukhov2025]. This measure considers competition for opportunities,
which prevents a single job opportunity from being available to more
than one person. Competitive measures matter when considering employment
outcomes because jobs are exclusive, and their use by one person
prevents their use by another. In addition, this measure relies on a
proportional allocation that balances the cost of travel and the
population size, imposing a constrained calculation that allocates the
opportunities to each origin. This ensures that, when all accessible
jobs are summed, the sum is equal to the total number of opportunities
in the region. Lastly, this measure is a more interpretable indicator
since it returns scores in the units of opportunities.

We calculated the multimodal spatial availability $V_i^m$ using Equation
(\ref{eq:spatial-availability-multimodal}):

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spatial-availability-multimodal}
V^m_{i} = \sum_{j=1}^J O_j\ F^{tm}_{ij}
\end{equation}

where:

-   $V^m_{i}$ is the spatial availability of opportunities at origin $i$
    and travel mode $m$;
-   $O_j$ is the number of opportunities at destination $j$;
-   $F^{tm}_{ij}$ is a balancing factor allocating opportunities at $j$
    to origin $i$ considering mode $m$.

$F^{tm}_{ij}$ incorporates both population demand and travel impedance,
defined according to Equation \ref{eq:multimodal-balancing-factors}:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:multimodal-balancing-factors}
F^{tm}_{ij} = \frac{F^{pm}_{i} \cdot F^{cm}_{ij}}{\sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{i=1}^N F^{pm}_{i} \cdot F^{cm}_{ij}}
\end{equation}

The population-based allocation factor is obtained by:

-   $F^{pm}_{i} = \frac{P_{i}^m}{\sum_{m}\sum_{i} P_{i}^m}$

Where $P_{i}^m$ represents the labour force at origin $i$ using mode $m$
competing for the opportunities $O$ at the destination $j$.

In turn, the travel impedance allocation factor is given by:

-   $F_{ij}^{cm} = \frac{f^m(c_{ij}^m)}{\sum_{m} \sum_{i} f^m(c_{ij}^m)}$

Where:

-   $c^m_{ij}$ is the cost to travel between $i$ and $j$ for mode $m$;
-   $f^m(c^m_{ij})$ is an impedance function representing the effect of
    travel cost.

## Modeling the relationship between objective accessibility, perceived accessibility, and employment outcomes

In this study, we aim to define minimum levels of objective
accessibility by identifying key thresholds in its relationship with
perceived accessibility and employment outcomes. The underlying
hypothesis of this strategy is that changes in the land-use and
transport characteristics of a neighbourhood, captured and represented
by objective accessibility, lead to changes in how residents perceive
their ability to reach job opportunities and in their reported
employment outcomes. We hypothesize that residents of neighbourhoods
with more (objective) accessibility are less likely to perceive job
scarcity or to report having declined job offers due to transport
constraints, independent of their individual demographic and
socioeconomic profiles. In our approach, we use objective accessibility
not as a causal exposure in itself, but as a proxy for the underlying
land-use and transport conditions that, as we hypothesize, shape
individual perceptions and outcomes.

Following the steps suggested by Huntington-Klein
[-@huntington-klein2021], we draw a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to
graphically represent our hypothesis (Figure \ref{fig:DAG}). DAGs show a
chain of hypothesized causal effects by using nodes to symbolize random
variables and arrows to represent the causal effect between two random
variables in the direction of the arrow [@cunningham2021causal;
@huntington-klein2021].

```{r DAG, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=paste0("Directed acyclic graph (DAG) of objective accessibility on perceived accessibility.")}

knitr::include_graphics(paste0(figures_diretorio,"/DAG_v2.png"))
```

We hypothesize that there is an association between objective
accessibility, perceived accessibility, and employment outcomes.
However, there are other ways in which they are connected, represented
by the other nodes of the diagram. First, there are mediator components
that influence the way a person perceives, or make use of, objective
accessibility. Each individual perceives the same neighbourhood
characteristics differently based on their capabilities and preferences,
as well as their travel options and experiences. For instance, a person
with a disability that prevents or makes it difficult for them to walk
or cycle will probably not enjoy the benefits of active accessibility to
the same extent as a person without such a disability
[@church_accessibility_2003]; someone without a car will not take
advantage of high car accessibility; someone without a monthly transit
pass might take less public transit than someone with a transit pass,
therefore reducing their potential for spatial interaction promoted by
higher public transit accessibility.

In addition, place of residence, and consequently an individual's
neighbourhood accessibility, is also influenced by socioeconomic
factors, with household income as the main driver of this decision, and
also by demographic characteristics (such as gender, race, citizenship,
among others). These socioeconomic and demographic factors not only
influence where someone will live, but also shape how individuals
experience travel and, consequently, make use of their neighbourhood
accessibility.

However, socioeconomic and demographic factors and the urban landscape
of the place of residence are also linked through a common cause ($U_1$)
that we cannot measure directly, such as generational wealth, which
likely influences both someone's neighbourhood and their income level.
Other unmeasured factors, such as residential self-selection and
adaptive preference, likely affect objective accessibility, perceived
accessibility, and employment outcomes ($U_2$).

Because other paths link objective accessibility to perceived
accessibility and employment outcomes, the observed association between
them cannot be assumed to reflect the true effect of accessibility on
how people experience and evaluate their access to employment
opportunities. If objective accessibility is to be used as a benchmark
or standard for equitable transportation planning, we believe it is
important to apply methods that aim to isolate its association with
perceived accessibility and employment outcomes, after accounting for
these confounding mechanisms, instead of relying on a raw statistical
association that may be inflated, offset, or masked by unobserved
individual preferences and constraints. Our approach relies on, first,
controlling for individual-level covariates capturing demographic,
socioeconomic, and travel-related characteristics; and second, applying
a framework using instrumental variables.

Guided by the diagram and the supporting literature, we identified
control variables corresponding to each node, following standard
causal-diagram identification methods [@cunningham2021causal;
@huntington-klein2021]. We selected the following variables:

-   Objective accessibility (treatment): multimodal spatial availability
    per person by transportation mode.
-   Perceived accessibility (outcome 1): agreement with *"there are too
    few jobs available for me in my ideal commuting time,"* obtained
    from NSTP.
-   Self-reported employment outcome (outcome 2): agreement with *"I
    have had to decline employment opportunities because of my transport
    situation,"* obtained from NSTP.
-   Travel attitudes, capabilities, and preferences: most used
    transportation mode; whether the preferred transportation mode
    matches the most frequent mode; whether the individual has a monthly
    or annual public transit pass; number of cars and bikes in the
    household; and whether the person has any disability, all obtained
    from NSTP.
-   Socioeconomic and demographic: whether the person is Indigenous or
    from a racialized population group; whether the person
    self-identifies as a woman; or as a transgender or non-binary
    person; age; household size and household income; and citizenship
    (temporary visa or refugee), all obtained from NSTP.
-   Urban landscape: population centre class (rural, small, medium, or
    large urban population centre) and population density (dissemination
    area level), obtained from Census.

In total, we estimate two regression models, one for each dependent
variable: perceived accessibility and declined job offers. Both models
use the instrumental variable approach described in the following
subsection, and each includes the three accessibility indicators
(active, public transit, and private vehicle spatial availability per
person), the interactions between active and transit accessibility and
their respective user indicators, and the full set of control variables
at the individual and household levels from the NSTP.

Although respondents expressed their level of agreement on a continuous
scale from 0 to 100, we treat these responses as ordinal measures, not
interval measures. Agreement scales based on sliders do not guarantee
that equal numerical differences reflect equal differences in
perception: a change from 10 to 20 may not represent the same variation
in agreement as a change from 80 to 90. Furthermore, respondents may use
the scale in different ways, for example, by grouping their responses
around the extremes or the midpoint. According to @liddell2018,
analyzing ordinal responses as if they were metric can distort the
estimated effects and inflate error rates. We can, however, have more
confidence in the order of the responses, since a respondent who selects
80 agrees more strongly than one who selects 60.

Therefore, using respondent weights, we transformed the dependent
variables into an ordered Likert scale based on their quintile position,
categorizing them as: "Most Negative", "Negative", "Neutral",
"Positive", and "Most Positive". The thresholds used for this
categorization are presented in Table \ref{tab:outcomes_quintiles}.
Since greater agreement with either statement indicates a worse
situation, the highest quintile of agreement corresponds to "Most
Negative". Quintiles also ensure a sufficient and balanced number of
respondents in each category, which is needed for stable estimation of
the ordinal models, and provide a middle category that serves as the
neutral reference for the dependent variable.

```{r outcomes-quintiles}
quintales <- read.csv(paste0(standards_measures_diretorio,"outcomes_quantile.csv")) %>% 
  filter(variable %in% c("FewJobs", "DeclineEmployment")) %>%
  mutate(Outcome = case_when(variable == "FewJobs" ~ "Few jobs available in my ideal commuting time", 
                             variable == "TravelTooLong" ~ "Travel too long to reach work", 
                             variable == "EasyToGo" ~ "Easy to reach work", 
                             variable == "DeclineEmployment" ~ "Declined job offers because of my transport situation")) %>% 
  dplyr::select(-c(variable,`X0.`)) %>% relocate(Outcome) %>% 
  kable(format = "latex", 
        booktabs = TRUE, 
        longtable = FALSE,
        caption = "\\label{tab:outcomes_quintiles}Quintile thresholds used to categorize dependent variables.", align = NULL,
    col.names = c("Outcome","20%","40%","60%","80%","100%")) %>%
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 10)

quintales
```

Considering that the outcome is an ordinal categorical variable, we used
weighted ordinal logistic regressions [@lumley2011] to model the
relationship between the objective accessibility indicators and the
categories of the dependent variables, using Equation
\ref{eq:ordinal-logit}:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ordinal-logit}
\log(\frac{P(Y\le j)}{P(Y > j)}) = \theta_j - (\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + ... + \beta_p X_p)
\end{equation}

\noindent where $Y$ represents the response category of the respondent
(ranging from "Most Negative" to "Most Positive"), and
$X_1, X2, ..., X_p$ represent the set of explanatory variables, and
$\theta_j$ and $\beta_p$ are unknown parameters to be estimated. The
parameters $\beta_p$ are constant for all outcome categories and measure
the change in the log-odds of reporting higher response categories
associated with each explanatory variable, while $\theta_j$ represents
the intercept separating the response categories.

Because of the high correlation between public transit and bicycle
accessibility (with Pearson correlation above 0.80), and because only 61
NSTP respondents (less than 3% of the sample) mentioned cycling as their
main commuting mode, we combined walking and cycling into a single
active transportation indicator, summing the jobs spatially available by
each mode. Including bicycle accessibility as a separate indicator,
given this small subsample and high collinearity with transit
accessibility, would likely have caused convergence problems when
creating our ordinal models. Fitting these models also requires a
sufficient number of respondents within each category and combination of
categories, which the small cycling subsample could not support.
However, we acknowledge that this combined active measure does not
account for the difference in travel speed between walking and cycling,
which can be substantial, and may understate the accessibility gains
cycling offers relative to walking over longer distances.

Table \ref{tab:var-description} presents the variables included in the
regression models and their descriptive statistics for the NSTP sample
(weighted mean and weighted standard deviation for continuous and dummy
variables, and weighted count and percentage for categorical variables,
created using the {gtsummary} `R` package [@gtsummary]).

### Instrumental variables

The presence of $U_2$ in our DAG implies the possibility of bias caused
by omitted variables that simultaneously affect objective accessibility,
perceived accessibility, and employment outcomes - a source of
endogeneity that compromises the consistency of the estimators
[@antonakis2010; @cunningham2021causal; @huntington-klein2021]. We
address this using an instrumental variable (IV) technique, where an
instrument $Z$ must be correlated with the outcome only through
objective accessibility. Examples of instrumental variables used in
studies analyzing the relationship between employment outcomes and job
accessibility include Euclidean distance from the spatial unit centroid
to the nearest major road or employment subcenter [@delmelle2021;
@jin2018], share of automobile ownership [@Hu2017], transit
accessibility and car unavailability [@johnson2017], distance to rivers
[@duarte2023; @luz2022], and population density [@bastiaanssen2021;
@bastiaanssen2025].

Two challenges arise in the search for relevant instruments: the
likelihood of correlation between instruments and the error term
increases with the strength of their correlation with the endogenous
variable, while instruments only weakly correlated with the endogenous
variable tend to perform poorly. Le Gallo and Páez [-@legallo2013]
developed an approach that relies on the use of synthetic instruments
derived from the spatial configuration of the data [see
@getis_comparative_2002; @griffith_spatial_2003], which ensures high
correlation with the treatment while, potentially, remaining exogenous
to the outcome. Following this approach:

1.  We built a queen-contiguity matrix for the census tracts to
    represent spatial weights, expressing the existence of a
    neighbouring relation as a binary relationship (1 for neighbours and
    0 otherwise).
2.  Then, we computed all eigenvectors associated with the contiguity
    matrix. These eigenvectors are orthogonal to one another and
    represent a portion of the variance in the spatial contiguity
    matrix.
3.  After this, we initialized a variable $S$ with value $0$ and
    linearly regressed each accessibility indicator (the independent
    variable) on each eigenvector and $S$. If the eigenvector
    coefficient was significant (adopting a p-value $\leq$ 0.05), we
    multiplied the eigenvector by its coefficient and added it to the
    value of $S$. After this process, $S$ represents the spatial filter
    associated with the accessibility indicator.

All spatial filters presented a Pearson correlation above 0.88 with
their respective accessibility measures and absolute correlations lower
than 0.15 with the original continuous dependent variables (before
transforming them into categorical variables), consistent with the
relevance and exclusion conditions required for valid instruments. In
addition, we performed Wald tests to evaluate the null hypothesis of
weak instruments and insufficient explanatory power to predict objective
accessibility, and Wu-Hausman tests to assess whether the accessibility
indicators are endogenous. We report both diagnostics for the
categorical models and, as a robustness check, for linear models
estimated on the original continuous dependent variables (Appendix
\ref{tab:iv-diagnostics}).

Since our dependent variables are not linear, the popular technique of
replacing endogenous variables by their first-stage predictors
(two-stage least squares estimation) is not appropriate - the so-called
"forbidden regression" in econometrics [@wooldridge2010;
@cunningham2021causal; @huntington-klein2021]. Therefore, we applied the
two-stage residual inclusion (2SRI) approach [@terza2008], in which, in
the first stage, we estimated the accessibility indicators using a
linear regression including all control variables plus spatial filters
(our instrumental variables). Next, in the second-stage, the dependent
variables were estimated using the accessibility measures, the control
variables, and the residuals from the first-stage regressions. Both
stages used respondent weights. In this approach, we use the regular
treatment to predict the outcome, but also control for the unexplained
part of the treatment.

## Identifying equity standards

Considering only the cases in which the objective accessibility was
statistically significant, we measured changes in the predicted
probabilities across response categories by varying the levels of
objective accessibility, while controlling for the other explanatory
variables. There are many possible ways of controlling the explanatory
variables (e.g., fixing the number of cars in the household as 0, 1, or
2+; or fixing the respondent age as 30, or 31, and so on). Based on
this, we decided to evaluate the effects of objective accessibility in
three distinct individual profiles:

-   A transport-disadvantaged profile, with individual-level control
    variables set to the values corresponding to populations facing the
    greatest transportation challenges.

-   The most prevalent profile, reflecting modal characteristics of the
    study area population and with control variables set to their most
    common values; and,

-   An advantaged profile, defined by selecting for the most privileged
    population segment in terms of their transport experience.

For each individual profile, we increased the value of each
accessibility measure by 0.01 jobs per person, while holding constant
other accessibility measures (representing alternative transportation
modes) at their weighted median values. We also adopted the weighted
median value for the population density and a constant zero value for
the residuals obtained from the first-stage regressions. For each
transportation mode, we evaluated the effect of accessibility by
considering the individual profiles as users of that specific mode. That
is, for active travel accessibility, all individual profiles were set as
active travellers, and so on for the remaining modes.

Then, for all individual profiles, we identified the minimum value of
objective job accessibility at which the combined probability of the
non-negative response categories ("Neutral", "Positive", and "Most
positive") exceeds the combined probability of the negative categories
("Negative" and "Most negative"). Because the five probabilities sum to
100%, this is equivalent to the probability of a negative response
falling below 50%. We name this value the conservative threshold. Next,
we defined the progressive threshold as the minimum accessibility value
at which the combined probability of the positive categories ("Positive"
and "Most positive") exceeds the combined probability of the negative
categories, excluding the neutral category from both sides. Finally, we
set the intermediate threshold as the midpoint between the conservative
and progressive thresholds.

We base our methodology on egalitarian and sufficientarian perspectives,
and we propose defining equity standards based on the
transport-disadvantaged profile. Our approach to operationalizing these
justice principles relies on identifying the minimum accessibility level
(sufficientarianism) at which the most disadvantaged profile
(egalitarianism) is more likely to give a non-negative response than a
negative one (conservative standard), and more likely to give a positive
response than a negative one (progressive standard).

## Measuring transportation equity

We calculated the extent and severity of accessibility gaps using FGT
measures [@foster2010], according to the Equation \ref{eq:FGT}. FGT
measures evaluate the number of people below a standard and the size of
the accessibility gap relative to it.

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:FGT}
FGT_\alpha = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{H}^{i=1}\left(\frac{z-y_i}{z}  \right)^{\alpha}
\end{equation}

Where $N$ is the size of the total population; $z$ is the accessibility
standard; $H$ is the number of individuals below the $z$; $y_i$ is the
accessibility level of each individual i; and $\alpha$: determines how
sensitive the index is to changes in the accessibility gap.

Changing the values of $\alpha$ enables the calculation of different FGT
indices [@karner2024]. When $\alpha = 0$, $FGT_0$ measures the extent of
undersupply as a simple headcount, indicating the proportion of people
below the standard. When $\alpha = 1$, $FGT_1$ measures the severity of
the undersupply as the average percent distance between the standard and
the accessibility levels of the individuals below it.

We applied the FGT measures to the general population in each CT, and
also to the population classified as low-income according to the Census,
as defined by the LIM-AT.

# Results and discussions

## Multimodal spatial availability per person.

Figure \ref{fig:multi-sa-pp} presents the maps with the multimodal
spatial availability of jobs per person. These maps show how, generally,
private vehicle users can access more job opportunities, but also show
that there is not much spatial variation when compared to the other two
modes, with most of the CTs in the study area classified in the
second-highest or highest accessibility categories. Toronto and
Mississauga present the highest level of private vehicle accessibility.

```{r multi-sa-pp, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.cap=paste0("Maps of the multimodal spatial availability per person, considering active, public transit and private vehicles (accessibility values are classified using quintile breaks).")}

knitr::include_graphics(paste0(figures_diretorio,"/SA_pp_3modes_v2_clipped.jpg"))
```

Transit accessibility appears to be more spatially distributed across
the study area, with the city of Toronto presenting the highest rate of
jobs accessible per transit commuters. Overall, we can observe an
expected spatial pattern where CTs close to public transit
infrastructure present higher levels of transit accessibility when
compared to suburbs and rural areas, which often lack public transit
services.

Next, the map of the active jobs accessible per active traveller
(walkers or cyclists) does not present a clear spatial pattern, with
many suburban and rural areas presenting higher levels when compared to
more urbanized areas. This can be explained by either a higher number of
jobs accessible within typical walking or cycling trip durations, less
probable; or, probably, because the number of active travellers in these
areas is very low, resulting in a higher rate of jobs per person, in a
way that higher accessibility values in these areas may reflect low
competition rather than higher absolute job availability.

Although private vehicle commuters represent about 78% of the labour
force, they compete for 96% of the jobs in the study area. Transit users
represent 15% of the labour force, but they reach only 3.4% of the jobs
available, while the remaining 0.6% of jobs available are competed for
by the 7% of active users. On average, each active user respondent from
the NSTP can access 0.06 jobs, while each transit user can access, on
average, 0.14 jobs. Both these measures are substantially lower than the
number of jobs that each private vehicle commuter can reach, which is
approximately one job per commuter on average.

## The impact of objective accessibility

Table \ref{tab:models} presents the two probability models linking
objective accessibility to perceived accessibility and employment
outcome. Based on Wald tests, we reject the null hypothesis of weak
instruments and insufficient explanatory power to predict our endogenous
variables (the objective accessibility indicators), as all F-statistics
are well above the Stock–Yogo critical values and statistically
significant (p-value \< 0.05). In the categorical models, the
first-stage residuals were non-significant in the second-stage
regressions, suggesting little evidence of endogeneity in the objective
accessibility indicators, and that standard regressions without the IV
approach could also have been appropriate. However, a Wu-Hausman test on
the linear (continuous) version of the employment-outcome model does
detect endogeneity (p \< 0.05; Appendix \ref{tab:iv-diagnostics}),
suggesting that the categorical model's failure to detect it may reflect
a loss of statistical power from quintile-categorization rather than
genuine exogeneity. Given this, we retained the IV framework throughout
our analysis rather than reverting to standard regressions.

```{r}
vars_model <- c("SA_pp_Active","SA_pp_Active:Active_user", "SA_pp_Transit", "SA_pp_Transit:Transit_user", "SA_pp_Car_motor", 
          "CarNumber", "BikeNumber", 
          "Match_mode", "TransitPass", "TransitAvailable", "Indigenous_or_racialized",
"Temporary_or_refugee",  "LongTermConditions", 
          "Woman_or_genderdiverse", "Age", "hh_size", "hh_income4", "Pop_density", "pc_class", "SA_pp_Active_Res_IV", "SA_pp_Transit_Res_IV", "SA_pp_Car_Res_IV")

single_row_models <- c("Match_mode", "Indigenous_or_racialized", "Temporary_or_refugee", "LongTermConditions", "Woman_or_genderdiverse", "TransitAvailable", "TransitPass", "SA_pp_Active:Active_user", "SA_pp_Transit:Transit_user")

glance_svyolr <- function(model){
  all_terms <- attr(terms(model), "term.labels")
  test_formula <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(all_terms, collapse = "+")))
  global_test <- regTermTest(model, test.terms = test_formula)
  f_stat <- global_test$F
  p_val <- global_test$p
  dev <- deviance(model)
  df_mod <- length(coef(model))
  n_obs <- nobs(model)
  aic <- dev + 2*df_mod
  bic <- dev + log(n_obs)*df_mod
  
  response_var <- all.vars(formula(model))[1]
  null_formula <- as.formula(paste(response_var, "~ 1"))
  null_model <- svyolr(null_formula, design = model$survey.design)
  dev_null <- deviance(null_model)
  mcfadden_r2 <- 1 - (dev/dev_null)
  
  tibble("F" = f_stat,
    "p.value" = p_val,
    "AIC" = aic,
    #"BIC" = bic,
    #"McFaddenR2" = mcfadden_r2
    )
}

fj_model_table <- few_jobs_model %>% 
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE,
                 include = vars_model, 
                 show_single_row = single_row_models, 
                 label = label_list, 
                 intercept = FALSE) %>% 
  add_glance_table(glance_fun = ~ glance_svyolr(.x),
                   label = list(F ~ "Wald F",
                                p.value ~ "p‑value",
                                AIC ~ "AIC"))%>%
  add_global_p() %>% 
  modify_header(label = "**Variable**") |>
  add_significance_stars(hide_p = FALSE, hide_ci = TRUE,  pattern = "{estimate}{stars}")  %>%
  remove_footnote_header(columns = estimate) %>% 
  modify_table_body( ~ .x %>% dplyr::mutate(significant = p.value < 0.05)) %>%
  modify_table_styling(columns = estimate,
    rows = significant == TRUE,
    text_format = "bold")
 
de_model_table <- decline_employment_model %>% 
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE,
                 include = vars_model, 
                 show_single_row = single_row_models, 
                 label = label_list, 
                 intercept = FALSE) %>% 
  add_glance_table(glance_fun = ~ glance_svyolr(.x),
                   label = list(F ~ "Wald F",
                                p.value ~ "p‑value",
                                AIC ~ "AIC"))%>%
  add_global_p() %>% 
  add_significance_stars(hide_p = FALSE, hide_ci = TRUE,  pattern = "{estimate}{stars}") %>%
  remove_footnote_header(columns = estimate) %>% 
  modify_table_body( ~ .x %>% dplyr::mutate(significant = p.value < 0.05)) %>%
  modify_table_styling(columns = estimate,
    rows = significant == TRUE,
    text_format = "bold")


combined_table <- tbl_merge(tbls = list(fj_model_table,  de_model_table),
    tab_spanner = c("**Few jobs**", "**Declined job offers**"))

combined_table_for_printing <- combined_table |>
  gtsummary::remove_abbreviation("CI = Confidence Interval") |> 
  as_kable_extra(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, full_width = FALSE, caption = "\\label{tab:models}Weighted ordinal logistic regression models connecting objective to perceived accessibility and to employment outcome." ) |>
  kableExtra::add_footnote(c("*p<0.05; **p<0.01; ***p<0.001.", 
                             "\nAccessibility indicators, population density, and first-stage residuals are standardized; odds ratios correspond to a one-standard-deviation increase."),
                           notation = "none", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)

combined_table_for_printing
```

Objective accessibility indicators were partially significant across the
models. Private vehicle accessibility did not present significant values
for any of the models, probably due to its ubiquity and homogeneity
across the study area.

The model related to the perception of job availability (i.e., "there
are too few jobs available for me in my ideal commuting time") produces
an estimated association consistent with our hypothesized causal
relationship, in which increases in objective transit and active
accessibility are associated with a higher probability of having a more
positive perception of accessibility. In fact, this is the model in
which the dependent variable is the most similar to the spatial
availability of jobs definition, which refers directly to the number of
jobs accessible, calculated using the impedance functions calibrated
based on population behaviour. For this model, a one-standard-deviation increase in transit accessibility (about 0.09 jobs per transit user) is associated with 25% higher
odds of being in a more positive response category, indicating that
fewer respondents agree that there are too few jobs accessible within
their ideal commuting time. Among non-active travellers, a one-standard-deviation increase in active accessibility (about 0.13 jobs per active traveller) is associated with 14% lower odds of being in a more positive response category. For
active travellers, on the other hand, the positive interaction term more
than offsets this, so the combined association is slightly positive. The
same occurs in the model related to declined job offers due to transport
constraints, whereby active accessibility is negatively associated with
outcomes for non-active travellers, but positively associated for active
travellers. We believe that the negative association between active
accessibility and responses among non-active travellers can be explained
in terms of job competition, since increasing the number of jobs
accessible for a mode that an individual does not use implies greater
competition for jobs accessible through other modes, effectively
reducing perceived accessibility for the mode a person actually uses. In
addition, as previously shown in Figure \ref{fig:multi-sa-pp}, many of
the areas with high active accessibility are located outside downtown
cores, in more suburban areas with a low concentration of job
opportunities. This reinforces the assumption that some suburban areas
exhibit high active accessibility not because of greater job
availability, but due to a very low number of active travellers,
resulting in a higher rate of jobs per person - reflecting low
competition for jobs accessible by walking and cycling rather than
higher active job availability.

Table \ref{tab:controls_pop} presents the control variable values
applied for each individual profile, while Figure
\ref{fig:transit-accessibility-thresholds} displays the specific effect
of increasing transit accessibility across the selected individual
profiles for the "few jobs available" model. For all of them, we observe
a decrease in negative perceptions as objective transit accessibility
increases. For the transport-disadvantaged individual profile, the "Most
negative" perception has a high probability at low levels of objective
accessibility. In fact, at the median objective transit accessibility
(0.12 jobs accessible by public transit per transit user, calculated
based on all NSTP respondents), the two most negative perception
categories ("Most negative" and "Negative") together account for over
52% of the total probability, resulting in a high likelihood that
individuals in the transport-disadvantaged group will have negative
perceptions at this accessibility level. For the most prevalent
population, the initial pattern appears similar to the
transport-disadvantaged group, but the decline in negative perceptions
occurs faster, with the combined probability of positive responses
("Positive" and "Most positive") surpassing that of negative responses
("Negative" and "Most negative") at approximately 0.28 jobs per transit
user. In contrast, for the advantaged population, we can see that even
at very low levels of accessibility, the positive perceptions already
present the highest probabilities and increasing transit accessibility
only reinforces these positive perceptions.
